title: Databricks Apps and application architecture
summary: Trace Cinderline's quality exception review app from browser to warehouse, Lakebase, endpoint and tool, choose the identity at each hop, bind resources and secrets, place state where it survives, validate before the app's grants are spent, and write mocked tests and a deployment guide labelled not deployed.
objectives: Trace one request through the front end, back end and data, model or tool hops of a Databricks App and name who authenticates and whose permissions apply at each boundary.

Choose app or user authorization per request, bind resources and secrets without a credential in code, take user context from the platform's headers, and place every piece of state where it must survive.
Validate a request before the app's grants are spent, assign incident ownership by evidence, and write a blueprint, mocked contract tests and a deployment guide labelled not deployed.

questions.prompt: In the claim trace, which identity does Lakebase evaluate for the insert, and how does the design keep a record of Imani?

options.text: The app's service principal, through its Postgres role; the handler writes Imani, taken from the forwarded header, into the claim row.
options.rationale: The Lakebase binding gives the app's principal a Postgres role, and the database sees only that role, so the handler records the reviewer.

options.text: Imani's own Postgres role, created when she first opened the app.
options.rationale: Opening an app creates no database role; the binding gives a role to the app's principal only.

options.text: The workspace admin's identity, because an admin created the app.
options.rationale: Creating an app grants the creator nothing inside it; the app's principal holds only what was granted to it.

options.text: No identity: Lakebase trusts every connection from inside the workspace.
options.rationale: Every Postgres connection authenticates as a role; there is no anonymous trusted path from the app.

questions.prompt: Imani's browser sends a claim whose inspection_key is A-2031' OR '1'='1. Which statement about sign-in and request validation is accurate?

options.text: Sign-in authenticates Imani and forwards the body unchanged; the back end's schema refuses it before any data call.
options.rationale: Authentication answers who is asking, never what the body contains, so the back end must validate the content.

options.text: Sign-in rejects the body because it contains a quote character.
options.rationale: The platform's sign-in does not inspect request bodies; content rules are the app's.

options.text: The warehouse rejects it, because the query runs as Imani, who lacks access.
options.rationale: Under app authorization the query would run as the app, whose grants are wider, which is why validation matters.

options.text: The browser strips the quote before sending, so no check is needed.
options.rationale: Any client can send any body; nothing on the browser side is a control the back end can rely on.

questions.prompt: Which value may stay in the app process's memory when the app can be restarted or redeployed at any time?

options.text: Manual text fetched from the manuals service, cached with an expiry.
options.rationale: Losing a cache costs one more fetch, and a slightly stale copy on another process is acceptable within the expiry.

options.text: The active claim on A-2031 revision 2.
options.rationale: A claim must be visible to every reviewer on every process and survive a redeploy, so it lives in Lakebase.
A disposition is an operational record that must be durable and change together with the item's status.

options.text: Imani's forwarded access token, kept for her next request.
options.rationale: A token is per-request: storing it risks serving her rights to someone else and must never happen.

cards.prompt: Which hop of a Databricks App does the reviewer's browser actually reach, and which part calls the warehouse?
cards.answer: The browser reaches only the app URL, where the platform signs the reviewer in; the app's back-end process is the only part that calls the warehouse, Lakebase, an endpoint or a tool.
cards.explanation: Frameworks such as Streamlit, Dash, Gradio, Flask, FastAPI and Node.js front ends differ in where the page is assembled, not in where credentials live. The browser holds no data credential and never meets the warehouse, which is why the permission question is always about the identity the back end uses.

cards.prompt: What is an app's service principal, and why can another app not reuse it?
cards.answer: A dedicated identity created for one app and unique to it; its grants define exactly what that app can reach, independent of any user.
cards.explanation: Because the principal belongs to one app, a grant made to Cinderline's quality app cannot leak to a second app or be inherited by the app's owner. Databricks injects its credentials as DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET, and under app authorization every downstream call runs as this principal, so the handler must decide what each reviewer sees.

cards.prompt: Why can a user-authorized app be refused an action the reviewer could perform in a notebook?
cards.answer: Because the app may act for a user only within the scopes it declared, such as sql, and Databricks blocks access outside approved scopes even when the user's own permissions are broader.
cards.explanation: Scopes bound the app, not the person. A new feature that needs another API means declaring another scope, which widens what the app can do on everyone's behalf and deserves the same review as any permission change. A missing scope is a fact to read on the app's configuration, not a fault in the reviewer's grants.

cards.prompt: How must the back end handle the X-Forwarded-Access-Token header on each request?
cards.answer: Read it from the current request, pass it only to the call that must run as the user, and never store, log, cache or share it; refuse the request if it is missing.
cards.explanation: The token carries one reviewer's rights. A module-level variable holding it hands those rights to another reviewer's concurrent request, a log line publishes it, and a silent fallback to the app when it is missing turns a per-user read into the app's wider read, which the agent authentication page warns about.

cards.prompt: Where does the handler get the reviewer's identity, and why not from the request body?
cards.answer: From identity headers the platform sets after sign-in, such as X-Forwarded-Email; the body is written by the client, so a body value naming someone else is refused.
cards.explanation: The application state design guide's ClaimRequest shows a reviewer field; in the running app the back end fills it from the header and treats a disagreeing body value as a forged request. Under app authorization Lakebase sees only the app, so the reviewer recorded on the row is the only record of who acted.

cards.prompt: What does binding a SQL warehouse as an app resource give the app, and what does it not give?
cards.answer: Can use on the warehouse for the app's principal and the warehouse ID in an environment variable through valueFrom; it grants no privilege on the tables queried through it.
cards.explanation: The binding is wiring plus a compute permission. Reading quality.raw.quarantine still needs Unity Catalog privileges on its catalog, schema and table for the app's principal, and a PERMISSION_DENIED naming the app on that table is a grant question for the data owner, never a code change.

cards.prompt: Where should the manuals-service token live, and where must it never appear?
cards.answer: In a secret scope, bound to the app as a secret resource and read from the environment at start; never in source, Git history, app.yaml values, the front end or logs.
cards.explanation: The environment also holds DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET, the app's own credentials, so a start-up line that prints the environment publishes both. Because the value is read once per process, a rotation is complete only after a restart or redeploy, and the old value is revoked last.

cards.prompt: Why can an in-memory claim map be wrong even when only one process serves the app?
cards.answer: Because a redeploy or restart replaces the process and empties its memory, and any second process has its own; a claim must be visible to everyone, so it belongs in Lakebase.
cards.explanation: Imani's claim in one process's dictionary is invisible to Leo's request on another process and gone after the next deployment, so both can claim the same item. The operational store keeps the claim and enforces one active claim per key and revision, which the module Lakebase, Postgres and operational state designs.

cards.prompt: Which parts of a Databricks App does the platform run, and which does the app team own?
cards.answer: Databricks provisions and manages the compute, the sign-in and the process start; the team owns the code, the start command, the dependencies, validation, handler checks and state placement.
cards.explanation: Nobody on the team sizes a cluster or patches a machine, but a redeploy or restart still starts a fresh process with empty memory. Compute size, language versions and any scaling options are read from the current environment documentation on the day of design, and the design stays correct whatever they are.

cards.prompt: How does requirements.txt decide which package versions the deployed app runs?
cards.answer: The deployment installs what requirements.txt lists, then runs the app.yaml command; an unpinned line resolves to whatever release is current on the day of the build.
cards.explanation: Packages installed on a laptop never travel with the app. An unpinned package that resolves to a newer release than the one tested is the classic works-locally failure; the deployment log's install step shows what was resolved, and pinning each direct dependency to the tested version fixes it.

cards.prompt: Why does request validation run before the handler spends the app's identity?
cards.answer: Because the app's principal holds grants the reviewer lacks, so every body is a lever on them; validation decides whether the privileged code runs at all.
cards.explanation: A schema with patterns, ranges and allowed values, a size limit and no unknown fields refuses an inspection key carrying an OR clause with a 422 before any query. Bound parameters are the second layer: even a missed rule cannot turn a value into SQL that the warehouse would run as the app.

cards.prompt: A claim body is valid, but the reviewer belongs to another plant. Which layer refuses it?
cards.answer: The handler's authorization check, because the Lakebase grant belongs to the app's principal and only the handler compares the reviewer's plants with the item's plant.
cards.explanation: Shape is the schema's job, permission the handler's and uniqueness the store's. A hidden button is not access control because any client can post the body, and a system prompt is not access control either. Whether the database could also enforce per-reviewer rules is recorded as the data lead's unknown.

cards.prompt: Who should open a slow-queue incident first, and when does it change hands?
cards.answer: The app team, reading the handler's timing in the app log; it moves to the warehouse owner only when that timing and the query history show the wait in the warehouse.
cards.explanation: Incidents follow evidence: a failed install is the deployment log and the app team's, a denial naming the app is a grant for the data owner, and a platform or sign-in failure goes to the platform team. Structured log lines with request id, reviewer and downstream timings make the first step possible.

cards.prompt: What changes for reviewers when files are synced to the workspace folder but not deployed?
cards.answer: Nothing: the running app keeps its previous deployment until a deploy builds the synced files, installs dependencies and runs the start command.
cards.explanation: The replayable sequence is bind, sync, deploy, build, start, verify, share and record. Declarative Automation Bundles, formerly Databricks Asset Bundles, declare the app and its resources per target so the same steps repeat in development and production. A guide nobody has run is labelled not deployed.

cards.prompt: What does a local mocked contract test prove about the quality app, and what can it not prove?
cards.answer: It proves the handler's request, response and error contract against fakes; it cannot prove grants, forwarded headers, the build, the port or database concurrency.
cards.explanation: FakeClaims returning claimed then conflict, and a fake plant lookup, exercise the real handler through a test client. A green suite says the contract holds, not that the app's principal can read the table, that the platform sends the headers the tests set, or that Postgres enforces one active claim under concurrent inserts.
